newsitem.title: GERMANY: German coalition MPs approve tax reform bill.
newsitem.headline: German coalition MPs approve tax reform bill.

text.p: Parliamentary deputies from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling coalition approved changes to the government's tax reform bill, virtually ensuring its passage through the lower house of parliament this week.

The changes, agreed by Kohl's coalition of Christian Democrats (CDU/CSU) and Free Democrats (FDP) late on Tuesday, include a number of last-minute modifications to corporate tax rules that have sparked a storm of protest from German industry.
"Ninety percent of companies are not affected by the new rules," said FDP parliamentary leader Hermann Otto Solms in defence of the measures.

The most controversial changes are a new rule making it more difficult for companies to reduce their tax liability by carrying forward losses from previous years and the introduction of a tax on hidden reserves for power utilities.
The changes met some opposition among pro-business FDP deputies, but the FDP parliamentary group as a whole approved the bill ahead of Thursday's official vote in the lower house.
Deputies from Kohl's Christian Democrats also questioned the changes affecting how a company handles losses, but they also approved the modifications in the end.
Hans-Olaf Henkel, president of the Federation of German Industry, told Reuters the changes were a populist move that would make it harder for German companies to compete.
"If this package is implemented things will get much worse," he said.

The changes would particularly hit companies that have counted on being able to carry forward losses, such as those who invested in eastern Germany, foreign investors and new companies who tend to run up losses in the beginning.

"We are very disappointed and deeply worried about how things are developing," he said. "It seems the ruling coalition is in a battle with the opposition to see who can put forward the most populistic tax proposal."
Ingrid Matthaeus-Maier, finance expert for the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), told the business daily Handeslblatt that protests from German industry were understandable.

The SPD is expected to block the tax bill when the opposition-controlled upper house of parliament votes on the bill on July 4. But Matthaeus-Maier said there were several points on which a compromise with the government could be reached, including the entry-level tax rate and the level of tax-free income.
Separately, the SPD plans to challenge in the Constitutional Court the way Finance Minister Theo Waigel has been constructing the federal budget, Handelsblatt reported.

The report said that Waigel's 1996 budget violated the constitution, which forbids the government from running a deficit that is higher than public investment. At the end of 1996, the federal deficit was 78.3 billion marks ($45.4 billion) and investment 61 billion marks, the report said.

The SPD parliamentary group approved a draft bill on Tuesday that aims to lower supplementary wage costs by reducing social security payments by two percentage points. The payments include contributions to unemployment insurance, as well as health and pension insurance.
In order to pay for the cut in unit wage costs, the SPD proposed raising petrol taxes by six pfennigs a litre.
